title: Top Espresso Machines for Home Baristas (2026)
summary: The De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is the best espresso machine for most people, with the Breville Bambino for small kitchens and the De'Longhi Stilosa for a tight budget.
method: Picks come from Tom's Guide (updated Aug 6, 2026; tested by a certified barista and a team of coffee experts) and TechRadar (updated Sep 18, 2026; Homes Editor Cat Ellis, an SCA-certified barista). The De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, Breville Bambino, De'Longhi Dedica Duo, KitchenAid Semi-Automatic and Ninja Luxe Cafe line show up in both outlets' coverage.
assumptions: Prices change often, so we quote list prices from the outlets' price boxes and tell you to check the current price. The outlets disagree in places: TechRadar names the Dedica Duo its best budget machine, while Tom's Guide rates it as good but pricey and prefers the cheaper Stilosa. Pick by how much work you want to do yourself.

products.name: De'Longhi La Specialista Touch
why: Tom's Guide calls it the best espresso machine for most people. A 3.5-inch touchscreen and De'Longhi's Bean Adapt system walk you through grind size, dosing and brewing, which tackles the cause of most bad shots from the start.
TechRadar also names it the best mid-range machine for anyone who wants to learn manual espresso, praising the same Bean Adapt guidance for first-timers.
specs: Semi-automatic with a built-in grinder (15 grind settings) and a guided tamping kit
19-bar pump; manual or automatic steam wand
3.5-inch touchscreen with drink presets, including cold brew
Tom's Guide price box shows a $799.95 list price; check the current price
pros: Guides beginners through grinding and tamping
Rich espresso with toffee and chocolate notes in Tom's test

Compact for a machine with a grinder

products.best_for: Beginners and improvers who want a smart, guided all-in-one machine
products.skip_if: You want a cheap starter machine or a fully hands-off experience

products.name: Breville Barista Touch Impress with Cold Extraction
why: TechRadar's best espresso machine overall, scoring 5 out of 5 for value, design and performance. It guides you through dosing and choosing a grind size, lets you tamp with a satisfying lever pull, then tells you if the shot ran too fast or slow and how to fix it.
The latest version also makes cold-brew-style coffee that TechRadar says tastes authentic, and the automatic milk system works well, especially with plant milk.

Automatic (AutoMilq) and manual steam wand
2-liter water tank
TechRadar's price box shows $1,499.95; check the current price

products.skip_if: You are happy with a manual machine, or you drink mostly full-fat dairy lattes

products.name: Breville Bambino
why: Tom's Guide gave its smallest, cheapest Breville a rare five-star review and names it the best compact machine. It has a PID controller for steady temperature, pre-infusion and one-touch single or double shots.

Its steam wand is flexible and powerful, it comes with a milk jug, and the reviewer called the espresso delectable. TechRadar likewise names the Bambino Plus, which adds automatic milk texturing, its best machine for small spaces.

About 13.7 x 6.3 x 12 inches; no built-in grinder

products.name: De'Longhi Stilosa
why: Tom's Guide's best machine under $150. The reviewer, a former barista, found it can pull consistently delicious shots with a little experimentation and one of the better steam wands at this price, capable of fine microfoam for lattes and flat whites.
It is very small and light, heats up quickly, and has a decent brewer under the plastic body.

products.name: De'Longhi Dedica Duo
why: TechRadar names it the best budget espresso machine it tested this year and says it beats most other sub-$300 alternatives. It is only 5.9 inches wide, heats quickly, holds pressure well and has an excellent steam wand.
New for this version is a cold-extraction option for smooth iced drinks. Tom's Guide rates it good but pricier than the Stilosa, so it only makes sense if you have very little counter space.

products.name: KitchenAid Semi-Automatic Espresso Machine
products.badge: Best for learning with a grinder
why: TechRadar's pick for hands-on espresso. Its flat-bottom 58mm portafilter sits steady on the counter, making tamping much easier, and the built-in burr grinder is impressively quiet. It produced rich espresso and silky microfoam from both dairy and oat milk.
Tom's Guide also rates it a high-quality mid-price machine, though it notes it lacks the automation of the Breville and De'Longhi models.

products.name: Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus
why: Tom's Guide's pick for beginners. It automates grinding, dosing and weighing, and auto grind-size calibration makes dialing in simple, so there is little trial and error.

You can froth milk automatically (with plant and dairy presets and even cold foam) or use the wand by hand. TechRadar also points to the Ninja Luxe Cafe as a cheaper alternative to the Breville with similar features, though less stylish.

why: Tom's Guide's best superautomatic. It grinds with conical burrs, then doses, tamps and brews at the touch of a button, and the reviewer found the shots reliably rich and consistent once his temperature, strength and volume were set.
It looks great, heats up quickly and has an easy interface. The catch is that it has no milk frother built in.

tips.title: How to choose
items: Decide how hands-on you want to be.
Manual machines like the Stilosa and Dedica Duo are cheapest but need skill. Guided machines such as the La Specialista Touch teach you as you go, and superautomatics do it all.

Tom's Guide calls the grinder the most important part of making espresso, so machines without one need a separate grinder, and a good one can cost $300 or more, though a hand grinder under $100 works for beginners.
Tom's Guide says the ideal pressure is 9 bar. A 15- or 20-bar rating just means headroom, not better coffee.
If you make lattes, look for a strong steam wand or an automatic system. TechRadar found the Barista Touch Impress froths plant milk better than full-fat dairy.

faq: What is the best espresso machine for most people?
Tom's Guide picks the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, while TechRadar names the Breville Barista Touch Impress with Cold Extraction its best overall.
Tom's Guide picks the cheaper Bambino and says the Plus adds automatic steaming but is slightly less good value. TechRadar names the Plus its best machine for small spaces.
Do I need a separate grinder?
Not with the La Specialista Touch, Barista Touch Impress, KitchenAid or Ninja Luxe Cafe, which have one built in. The Bambino, Stilosa and Dedica Duo do not.
What if I want to go deeper into espresso?

Tom's Guide recommends the Gaggia Classic E24 for enthusiasts. It is manual with a brass boiler and group head but no PID, so you manage the temperature yourself. For premium, it picks the Fellow Espresso Series 1.
